### 4.5.1 – Turning Situations Into Equations

Linear models describe real situations where one quantity changes at a constant rate.
The slope is the **rate**, and the intercept is the **starting value**.

:::{.example title="Example – Babysitting Pay"}
A babysitter earns $12 per hour plus $10 for transportation.
[
f(x) = 12x + 10
]

* (m = 12): pay rate per hour
* (b = 10): base fee
  :::

:::{.you-try title="Write a Rule"}
You earn $8 per hour mowing lawns and start with $20 already saved.
Write an equation for your total savings after x hours.
:::

---

### 4.5.2 – Negative Slopes: Decreasing Situations

Not all relationships increase.
Some, like cooling or spending, have **negative slopes**.

:::{.real-world title="Example – Cooling Water"}
A cup of coffee cools from 90°C to 60°C over 10 minutes.
[
f(x) = -3x + 90
]

* (m = -3): the coffee cools 3°C per minute
* (b = 90): starting temperature
  :::

:::{.you-try title="Describe the Meaning"}
In (f(x) = -5x + 100), what does the slope tell us?
What does the intercept mean?
:::

---

### 4.5.3 – Interpreting Slope and Intercept

:::{.real-world title="Example – Cell Phone Bill"}
A phone plan costs $50 per month plus $0.10 per text.
[
f(x) = 0.10x + 50
]

* (m = 0.10): cost per text
* (b = 50): base monthly charge
  :::

:::{.think title="Why Units Matter"}
Slope and intercept should always have **units** — they tell what’s changing and what’s fixed.
:::

:::{.you-try title="Explain the Meaning"}
The equation (f(x) = 4x + 15) models parking costs, where x is hours.
What do 4 and 15 represent?
:::

---

### 4.5.4 – Estimating Best-Fit Lines

Sometimes real data isn’t perfectly linear — but we can find a **line that fits “about right.”**

1. Plot data points on a scatter plot.
2. Sketch a line that seems to match the trend.
3. Write a rule that fits the pattern roughly.

![](/images/Unit_4/Lesson_5/scatter_best_fit.png){width="360px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.real-world title="Example – Height vs. Age"}
Students measure their height each year.
The points don’t make a perfect line, but a line through the middle of the points shows the average growth rate.
:::

:::{.you-try-m title="Draw a Best-Fit Line"}
Your teacher will provide data for shoe size vs. age.
Plot the points and sketch a best-fit line.
Estimate the slope and intercept and write an equation.
:::

:::{.think title="When Two Models Cross"}
Sometimes two linear trends meet — for example, when expenses catch up to income,  
or when two cars traveling at different speeds reach the same distance.  
That crossover point means the two equations give the same output.  
:::

---

:::{.remember title="Key Idea"}
Linear models show **constant rates of change** in real situations.

* The **slope** represents the rate.
* The **intercept** represents the starting value.
* Using (f(x)) reminds us that outputs depend on inputs.
  :::
